questions.question: What is ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and how do you prevent it?
questions.title: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException in Java
questions.direct_answer: `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` is a `RuntimeException` thrown when you try to access an array index that does not exist — either negative or equal to/greater than `array.length`. It is prevented by always looping with `i < arr.length` and checking bounds before direct access.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand valid array index range and can identify the classic off-by-one mistake in a loop.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing `i <= arr.length` instead of `i < arr.length` in a for loop — this is the most common cause by far.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that it is an unchecked RuntimeException (extends IndexOutOfBoundsException → RuntimeException), so the compiler never warns you — only happens at runtime.

sections.title: Why Asking for the Sixth Slot of a Five-Slot Array Crashes
sections.content:
Every element in an array has a position number, and in Java those numbers start at `0`. That position is called the **index** — the first element is `arr[0]`, the second is `arr[1]`, and so on.

This is where one of the most common beginner crashes comes from: **the indices run from `0` to `length − 1`, not `1` to `length`**. A five-element array has slots `0, 1, 2, 3, 4`. There is no slot `5`.

When you ask for a slot that does not exist — `arr[5]` on that array — Java checks the index against the array's length while the program runs, sees it is out of range, and throws **`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`**. Think of it as Java refusing to read past the end of the block rather than handing you whatever random memory happens to sit there, which is what C would do.

Why doesn't the compiler catch this for you? Because **the index is almost always a variable** — `arr[i]`, where `i` is worked out while the program runs. The compiler has no way to know what `i` will be, so the check has to happen live, on every single access.

One nuance worth saying out loud: this is an **unchecked** `RuntimeException`. Nothing forces you to wrap it in a try-catch; the code compiles cleanly and simply crashes the moment it fires.

The classic gotcha is a loop written `i <= arr.length` instead of `i < arr.length`. **That one extra `=` lets `i` reach `5`**, and `arr[5]` blows up. A negative index like `arr[-1]` throws too — unlike Python, Java has no notion of counting back from the end.

sections.title: Valid Index Range for a 5-Element Array
sections.content:
Valid indices are always 0 to length−1. One step beyond either end throws the exception. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["access arr[i]"] --> B{"i >= 0 AND
i < arr.length?"} B -->|"yes"| C["access element
— safe"] B -->|"no"| D["ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
thrown at runtime"] ``` For `int[] arr = new int[5]`: valid is 0–4. Trying `arr[5]` or `arr[-1]` both trigger the exception.

sections.title: The Classic Off-By-One Mistake — and the Fix
Picking the Loop That Can't Go Out of Bounds
sections.content:
**When you only need to read each element** and don't care about its position, use the enhanced for loop — `for (int x : arr)`. There is no index to mismanage, so it physically cannot throw `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. Make this your default for read-only traversal.

**Reach for a classic indexed `for` loop** only when you actually need the index:

- to write back into the array
- to compare neighbouring elements
- to step by more than one

There, always write `i < arr.length`, never `<=`, and never hardcode the upper bound.

When you access a single element from a variable index — say, a number that came from user input or a calculation — guard it with `if (i >= 0 && i < arr.length)` before you touch the array. The rule that keeps you safe is simple: **validate the index first, index second**.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`i <= arr.length` in a loop** — the extra `=` runs one more iteration and reads `arr[length]`, which never exists. This single typo causes the large majority of these crashes.
- **Assuming negative indexing works** — `arr[-1]` does not mean "last element" like in Python; it throws immediately. The last element is `arr[arr.length - 1]`.
- **Hardcoding an index** — `arr[10]` on an array that might hold three elements crashes; guard any variable index with a bounds check first.
- **Catching it instead of fixing it** — wrapping the access in try-catch hides the off-by-one rather than correcting the loop. The bug is the index logic, not a recoverable runtime condition.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Valid range is `0` to `arr.length - 1`** — a 5-element array has no element at index 5.
- **Off-by-one in loops**: `i <= arr.length` is the #1 cause — always use `i < arr.length`.
- **Use enhanced for when you don't need the index**: `for (int x : arr)` is guaranteed safe.
- **Unchecked exception**: extends `RuntimeException` — the compiler never warns you; it crashes at runtime.
- **Negative indices also throw it**: unlike Python, Java has no concept of `arr[-1]` for last element — use `arr[arr.length - 1]`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The crash everyone hits on the very last loop iteration is the way into this one. **Array indices in Java start at zero**, so a five-element array's last valid index is four, not five — and `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` is what you get the moment you reach outside that `0` to `length − 1` range.

The compiler can't catch it because the index is usually a variable that's only known at runtime, and it's an **unchecked `RuntimeException`**, so nothing forces you to handle it — it just crashes when it fires. **By far the most common cause** is a loop written `i <= arr.length` instead of strictly less-than, which runs one iteration too many.

So I always loop with `i < arr.length`, and when I only need to read the values I reach for the **enhanced for loop**, since with no index there's nothing to get wrong. For a single lookup from a variable, I guard it with a bounds check first.

And unlike Python, **Java has no negative indexing** — the last element is `arr[arr.length − 1]`, never `arr[-1]`.

speakable_v2.hook: That crash on the very last loop pass? It almost always traces to one character — a `<=` where you meant `<`.

groups.heading: Indexed for loop
groups.text: You manage `i` yourself, looping while `i < arr.length`. It's flexible, but you own the bounds.

groups.heading: Enhanced for loop
groups.text: `for (int x : arr)` hands you each element. There's no index, so there's nothing to push out of range.

items: Reach for the enhanced loop whenever you're only reading each element.
Use the indexed loop to write back, compare neighbours, or step by more than one.
For a single lookup, guard it with `if (i >= 0 && i < arr.length)` first.

beats.text: With `int[] s = {90, 85, 78}`, writing `i <= s.length` runs one pass too many, so `s[3]` throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. The **gotcha**? It's off-by-one, not a deep bug.

speakable_v2.cap: So loop with `i < arr.length`, and prefer the enhanced for when you don't need the index at all.
